summary: Switzerland is not in the EU but joins the Schengen Area through association agreements: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities can stay 90 days in any 180-day period (with the ETIAS travel authorization being phased in), and everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa (the €90 fee is charged in Swiss francs, about CHF 90).

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

source.name: European Commission — Schengen short-stay calculator (DG Migration and Home Affairs)

fee.notes: Equivalent of the EU-wide €90 fee, charged in Swiss francs (amount adjusted with the exchange rate). Children 6–11 pay half; under 6 free.
Approximate. For stays over 90 days (residence, family reunification); requires prior authorization from the cantonal migration authority.
Approximate. For courses longer than 90 days; the cantonal migration authority must approve the stay before the visa is issued. Proof of enrollment, funds and accommodation required.
Approximate. The Swiss employer must first obtain a work permit from the canton; annual quotas apply to non-EU/EFTA workers, and priority is given to the domestic labor market.

passportValidity.text: Non-EU/EFTA passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area and have been issued within the last 10 years.

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000 (roughly CHF 28,000–30,000), valid across the Schengen Area for the whole stay. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it, but Swiss healthcare is expensive — cover is strongly recommended.

onwardTicket.text: Border officers may ask non-EU/EFTA visitors for proof of return or onward travel and accommodation details.

proofOfFunds.text: Switzerland uses a guideline of around CHF 100 per person per day for visitors (CHF 30 for students), shown in cash, cards or bank statements if asked.

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Switzerland participates in the EU Entry/Exit System as a Schengen associate: non-EU travelers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) at Schengen external borders, including Swiss airports. Registration happens at the border — allow extra time on your first entry.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorization System

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: ETIAS will also apply to Switzerland as a Schengen associate: visa-exempt travelers will need the authorization to enter. It is being phased in — check the official EU site for the current status and apply only there.

currencyLimits.text: Unlike the EU, Switzerland has no obligation to declare cash. However, customs officers can ask anyone carrying CHF 10,000 or more (or equivalent) about their identity and the origin, intended use and beneficial owner of the money — refusing to answer or giving false information is an offense, and the amount is recorded.

source.name: FOCBS (Swiss customs) — cash, foreign currency, securities

notes: Switzerland is outside the EU customs union: allowances apply even when arriving from EU neighbors — 250 cigarettes, 5 liters of alcohol up to 18% and 1 liter above 18% per adult per day.
Goods worth more than CHF 150 per person per day are subject to Swiss VAT on the full value.

payments.text: Cards, contactless and the local TWINT app are accepted almost everywhere. Euros are often taken in shops and stations, but at unfavourable rates with change given in francs — pay in CHF.

safety.text: Switzerland is one of the safest countries in the world, with very low crime. Petty theft can occur around train stations and tourist sights; in the mountains, the main risks are weather and terrain — check conditions before hiking.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Switzerland Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: June–September for hiking, lakes and mountain railways; December–February for winter sports. Shoulder months can leave high-altitude routes and some resorts closed.

roadVignette.appliesTo: All motor vehicles and trailers up to 3.5 t; a towed trailer needs its own vignette.
roadVignette.text: Switzerland sells exactly one vignette: CHF 40, valid for 14 months from December 1 of the previous year to January 31 of the following one. There are no short-term options, so a single motorway trip costs the full CHF 40. You can choose the e-vignette linked to your number plate (e-vignette.ch) or the sticker on the windscreen; both cost the same. Buy it before entering the country — only at Basel St. Louis, Rheinfelden and Kreuzlingen may you use the motorway without one, and only as far as the first exit.

source.name: Federal Office for Customs and Border Security (FOCBS) — Motorway charge FAQ

idp.text: Switzerland is a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1949 Geneva one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1968 Vienna version. A permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Vienna, 1968), status of parties
source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Vienna, 8 November 1968 (UNTS vol. 1042, p. 17)

driving.text: Switzerland is a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1949 Geneva one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1968 Vienna version. A permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Switzerland yet.

tips.text: The 90-day limit counts across the entire Schengen Area, not just Switzerland — days spent in France or Italy count against the same allowance.
Switzerland is one of the world's most expensive destinations — budget roughly double what you would spend in neighboring countries; a simple lunch can cost CHF 20–30.
Driving on Swiss motorways requires an annual vignette (CHF 40, sticker or e-vignette) — buy it at the border, post offices or online before taking a motorway; fines are far higher than the vignette.
Switzerland uses its own type J sockets: slim two-pin Europlugs (type C) fit, but the chunky grounded type F plugs common in the EU do not — bring an adapter.

faq.question: Is Switzerland in the EU or the Schengen Area?
faq.answer: Switzerland is not an EU member, but it is part of the Schengen Area through association agreements, so the same short-stay visa rules apply as in the EU Schengen states. It is outside the EU customs union, so customs allowances apply even when arriving from EU neighbors.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Switzerland?
faq.answer: No. US passport holders can visit Switzerland and the rest of the Schengen Area visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, they will need to obtain this online authorization (€20) before travel.

faq.question: How much does a Switzerland Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: The Schengen short-stay visa fee is €90 for adults (half for children 6–11), charged by Swiss representations in Swiss francs — about CHF 90, adjusted with the exchange rate. It allows stays of up to 90 days in any 180-day period across all Schengen countries.

faq.question: Do I have to declare cash when entering Switzerland?
faq.answer: There is no obligation to declare cash on entry, unlike in the EU. However, if you carry CHF 10,000 or more (or equivalent), customs officers can require you to disclose your identity and the origin, intended use and beneficial owner of the money — refusing or lying is a customs offense.

faq.question: Do I need a vignette to drive in Switzerland?
faq.answer: Yes — using Swiss motorways requires a vignette costing CHF 40, valid for the calendar year (plus a grace period), available as a windscreen sticker or e-vignette registered to your plate. Driving on a motorway without one incurs a CHF 200 fine plus the vignette cost.
